title: The Cappadocians
hookLine: Basil and the two Gregorys gave the words for three persons in one being

cards: Ask the money-changer for change, and he lectures you about the Begotten and the Unbegotten. Ask the baker the price of bread, and he tells you the Father is greater and the Son is less.

Ask whether the bath is ready, and the attendant informs you that the Son was made from nothing. That's Gregory of Nyssa, in a sermon, complaining about a great city where everyone seemed to have an opinion about God.
The arguments over the Trinity weren't happening only in libraries. They were happening at the market. Today, the people who sharpened the church's words: the Cappadocians.

teach.b: Cappadocia is a region in what is now central Turkey. From there came Basil of Caesarea, his brother Gregory of Nyssa, and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus.
Gregory of Nyssa also wrote about their sister Macrina as a teacher in her own right. The question they faced was old; this path first met it on day two hundred ninety-nine.
Jesus sends his disciples out baptizing "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost."
One name, three named. So is God one or three? The Cappadocians answered with two Greek words, and gave each a separate job.
Ousia, being: what God is. There is one. Hypostasis, person: who God is.
There are three, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. One being, three persons. Not three gods working as a team.

Not one God wearing three masks. They offered comparisons, like three people sharing one human nature, and then warned that every comparison falls short, because God is not one more thing in the world.

teach.h: LIT BY THE THREE, BACK TO THE ONE.
teach.b: Gregory of Nazianzus put the experience of it this way, in paraphrase: no sooner do I think of the One than I'm lit up by the Three; no sooner do I tell the Three apart than I'm carried back to the One.
Their words helped shape how the Nicene Creed came to be understood. For them, the Trinity was not a puzzle to solve. It was a mystery to stand inside.

how: Churches confess one God in three persons in the Nicene Creed, baptize in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and close prayers and blessings by naming all three; Orthodox and Catholic churches honor Basil and the two Gregorys as saints and teachers.

games.q: three and one — tap the pairs.

s: the Cappadocians taught three gods working as a team
one being, three persons. not three gods, and not one God wearing three masks.
Basil and Gregory of Nyssa were brothers
and Gregory of Nazianzus was their friend. Gregory of Nyssa also wrote of their sister Macrina as a teacher.
arguments about the Trinity stayed in libraries
Gregory of Nyssa complained that even money-changers and bakers argued about it.

games.q: someone at the market asks you: is God one, or three? what do you answer?
o: one. the three are just masks.
games.why: the Cappadocians helped give the church those words: one ousia, being, and three hypostases, persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

practice: Christians have an old blessing from Paul that names all three: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all."
If you pray, say it slowly, letting each name land, grace, love, communion; if you don't, just listen to the shape of it, three names, one blessing, given to everyone at once.

wordCard.voice: The Cappadocians. Basil and the two Gregorys, who helped give the church its words for the Trinity: one being, three persons.

orig.note: Greek: being, what God is. the Cappadocians spoke of one ousia in three hypostases, persons.
